Welcome to the Classroom!

Whatever your level of experience, if you have a query, this is where you'll find many people to help you answer it. There's no such thing as a stupid question, and you can be sure that if you wonder about something, there are others who wonder the same and will be glad you aired it. There's lots of homework set for you to do. If you'd like help getting started with it, feel free to post your first couple of examples here for critique, before you do the rest and put them in your journal.

To perpetuate the "Traders helping Traders" philosophy, once you've learned concepts and understand them fully, you're encouraged to share what you've learned with those who come behind you. This is not just good for them, but will help concrete your own understanding of the material, so after you've learned by learning, you'll then learn by teaching!

None of us have the time to answer queries by PM, so please use this room to learn together as a group. We're sure you'll find friends for life in here!

Hello narottam178, I have found it necessary to analyze the charts from HTF to LTF. If you just open up a 15M chart and only trade zones you see in that time frame you will surely get burned as price will often disrespect your treasured zones. It is crucial to look at the LTF in the context of the HTF. So I would say it is not prudent to trade s/d zones from one time frame only. If you see price trending up on daily/H4 time frame then looking for retrace to demand seems reasonable. Once you get close to a demand zone then looking at the lower time frames for entry is the ticket.

If you're here to learn, post a chart of your mistakes. Indicate where you took the trade, why, and your targets. Let the forum add their input. At the very least, start a trading journal and record the history of good and bad trades. Figure out why and how the good ones worked and why the bad ones didn't. But be specific, it'll tedious but will help you.

On a side note, it is vey difficult to replicate live trading on a demo. A demo is good to try new concepts etc but it will never teach you the mindset needed to enter and exit trades. However, if you learn supply and demand trading well AND trust it, it helps takes those wicked emotions away.

Good luck.

Good question. I'm a big fan of correlating pairs. I think it serves as a good indicator. First is to realize how one pair correlates to another. Then you watch the levels like you would any other trade. For example, this past Friday, on the GU & EU moved closed together. Watch when one pair reacted at a level then other followed. Also look at the crosses for a good indication. The EURGBP was a good indictor on Friday. AU and NU was also an easier pair to correlate. There's a benefit to trading the pair that slightly lags, just make sure you're trading the levels according to that pair. Meaning that, let's say, demand was 50 pips away on the leading pair and only 25 pips away on the lagging pair, target the 25 pips if trading the lagging pair not the 50 pips as indicated on the leading pair. Hope that helps.

It's always best to be aware of which currency is going to cause the turn

If you want to, say, sell GU, you should know whether it's because of the dollar getting ready to rise, or the pound to fall Looking at the dollar pairs will tell you if it's the former, in which case you'll look for the pair with the best setup and room to move

If not, look at the various pound pairs, and if GBP is in Supply all round, you'll know that the turn will be due to oncoming pound weakness, making it the ideal time to sell

In essence, always be aware of who is about to turn the market
